source_caption:
Most of the street interactions with men in Under the Skin weren’t scripted. To capture the rawest human instinct possible, director Jonathan Glazer rigged Scarlett Johansson’s van with 8 hidden cameras and sent her onto the streets of Glasgow (Scotland). Most of the men she approaches in the movie weren't actors; they were random strangers who had no idea they were being filmed. Scarlett had to improvise every conversation, luring them into the van while the crew watched from a secret trailer nearby. It wasn't until after the scenes were shot that the crew would jump out and ask for consent to use the footage. 

Jonathan Glazer used hidden cameras and real, unsuspecting men in Under the Skin for one core reason: authentic human behavior cannot be performed.The movie uses hidden cameras to prove that "under the skin," what actually makes us human isn't our looks or our lust, but our ability to feel empathy.

Adding to its eerie impact is Mica Levi’s experimental score, now considered one of the most haunting soundtracks of the decade. Under the Skin divided audiences, but it cemented itself as a cult classic a film that doesn’t explain itself, doesn’t reassure you, and never lets you forget it.

Usually, women are the ones being hunted in movies. Here, Scarlett uses the 'Male Gaze' as a weapon to lure men into a void. It’s a mirror for how we objectify people based on what’s 'on the skin.' What did you think of the ending? 
.

source_details.title: Under the Skin
source_details.synopsis: Under the Skin is a 2013 science fiction film directed by Jonathan Glazer and written by Glazer and Walter Campbell, based on the 2000 novel by Michel Faber. It stars Scarlett Johansson as an extraterrestrial disguised as a human who preys on lone men in the evening hours in Scotland. Glazer developed Under the Skin for over a decade. He and Campbell pared it back from an elaborate, effects-heavy concept to a sparse story focusing on an alien perspective of the human condition. Most of the cast had no acting experience, and many scenes were filmed with hidden cameras. The film premiered at the Telluride Film Festival on 29 August 2013. It was released in the United Kingdom on 14 March 2014,
